prelimsCapsule.coreConceptSummary: The Parliament of India is the supreme legislative body representing the people's will in a Westminster-style parliamentary democracy. It comprises the President of India and two houses (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha), functioning as the bedrock of accountability and constitutional evolution.
highYieldFacts: Fact 1: Under Article 79, Parliament consists of the President, the Council of States (Rajya Sabha), and the House of the People (Lok Sabha).
Fact 2: The President is an integral part of Parliament but does not sit in either House to participate in discussions.
Fact 3: Rajya Sabha (Council of States) acts as a chamber of continuity, while Lok Sabha (House of the People) provides democratic legitimacy.
Fact 4: The 'Bicameral' structure is a feature borrowed from the British Constitution, modified to suit India’s federal character.
Fact 5: Parliamentary sovereignty in India is qualified by the doctrine of 'Judicial Review' and the 'Basic Structure' of the Constitution.
trapsAndElimination: Trap 1: Assuming the President sits in Parliament sessions; they are part of Parliament but not a member of either house.

mainsFramework.inDepthTheoryHtml:
The Constitutional Architecture of Parliament

The Indian Parliament is not merely a law-making body but the heartbeat of India's representative democracy. Operating under the principle of Parliamentary Sovereignty constrained by Constitutional Supremacy, its design reflects a nuanced balance between efficiency and deliberation.

  • Trifurcated Structure: Article 79 mandates the President as an integral component, ensuring that no bill becomes an act without executive-legislative consensus (Assent).
  • Bicameralism: The Rajya Sabha serves as a federal chamber representing states, preventing 'hasty legislation,' while the Lok Sabha represents the direct mandate of the citizenry.
  • Checks and Balances: Through mechanisms like Question Hour, Zero Hour, and Standing Committees, Parliament enforces executive accountability (Article 75(3) - collective responsibility).

Contemporary Challenges

Modern parliamentary discourse faces severe attrition in functionality:

  • Legislative Erosion: Increasing usage of Ordinances and 'Money Bill' route (avoiding Rajya Sabha scrutiny) undermines the spirit of federalism.
  • Policy Decimation: Reduced frequency of sessions and the declining referral of bills to Departmentally Related Standing Committees (DRSCs) limit the depth of legislative scrutiny.
  • Ethics & Conduct: The rise of 'legislative dysfunction' and frequent adjournments impede the time available for crucial policy debate.

dimensions.constitutional_or_legal: Evolution of Parliamentary Privileges (Article 105) and the limitation of legislative power via Basic Structure Doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati case).
dimensions.socio_economic: Representation of marginalized sections (SC/ST reservation in Lok Sabha) and the role of Parliament in addressing socio-economic inequalities.
dimensions.administrative_governance: The transformation from mere legislation to 'oversight' functions, including Audit and Expenditure control via PAC and Estimates Committee.
dimensions.international_or_comparative: Comparison with the British Model (sovereign parliament) versus India (written constitution as the ultimate source of power).

landmarkJudgmentsOrReports: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973): Established Basic Structure Doctrine.
Raja Ram Pal v. Hon'ble Speaker, Lok Sabha (2007): Supreme Court upheld the power of Parliament to expel members for breach of privilege.
2nd ARC Report on 'Ethics in Governance': Recommends internal institutional mechanisms to check parliamentary disruptions.
NITI Aayog Strategy for New India: Recommends strengthening the Committee system for higher legislative quality.

prelims.question: With reference to the Parliament of India, consider the following statements: 1. A private member’s bill is a bill presented by a Member of Parliament who is not elected but only nominated by the President of India. 2. Recently, a private member’s bill has been passed in Parliament for the first time in its history. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
prelims.explanation: A private member is any MP who is not a minister. Both elected and nominated members can introduce private member bills. No private member's bill has been passed since 1970.

modelMainsQA.question: Critically analyze the role of the Parliament of India in ensuring executive accountability and upholding constitutional morality in contemporary times. (250 Words, 15 Marks)

approach.intro: Define Parliament as the central pillar of Indian Democracy under Article 79, mentioning the 'Trifurcated' nature and its role as the conscience of the nation.
approach.body: Discuss the 'Accountability' mechanism (Question Hour, Committees). Then, highlight 'Contemporary Challenges' (Ordinance Raj, Money Bill misuse, lack of debate). Use constitutional morality as a benchmark.
approach.conclusion: Suggest strengthening the Committee system, adopting a code of conduct for members, and ensuring fiscal oversight to preserve the parliamentary ethos.

modelMainsQA.modelAnswerHtml:
Role of Parliament: Accountability vs. Dysfunction

The Parliament of India, as per Article 79, is not just a law-making body but the institutional crucible of executive accountability. Through the principle of collective responsibility, it serves as the ultimate check on the executive branch.

1. Mechanisms of Accountability

  • Legislative Scrutiny: Through Departmentally Related Standing Committees (DRSCs), Parliament performs a 'micro-level' analysis of budgetary allocations and policy outcomes, away from partisan floor debates.
  • Question Hour: Acts as the 'Sword of Damocles' over the executive, forcing transparency on daily governance issues.

2. Contemporary Challenges to Constitutional Morality

  • Circumvention: The increasing use of the 'Money Bill' route (e.g., Aadhaar Act, Tribunals Reform Act) to bypass the Rajya Sabha risks undermining the bicameral check-and-balance system.
  • Legislative Attrition: Decline in the number of working days and frequent disruptions result in bills being passed without adequate debate, violating the spirit of 'deliberative democracy.'

3. The Way Forward

To uphold constitutional morality, Parliament must:

  • Mandate Committee Scrutiny: Make it mandatory to refer all major legislative bills to the relevant Standing Committees.
  • Shadow Cabinet Approach: Encourage more structured opposition participation in policy formulation.
  • Digital Accountability: Utilize technology to track real-time legislative participation and performance to increase public scrutiny.

Conclusion: The Parliament is the custodian of the 'Basic Structure' of our Constitution. Restoring its dignity through disciplined conduct and rigorous legislative scrutiny is essential for the longevity of the democratic project in the 'Amrit Kaal.'

practiceMCQs.question: Which of the following is correct regarding the 'Concept of Parliament' in India?
options: Parliament consists of Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha, and the Prime Minister
The President is an integral part of Parliament but does not participate in the business of either house
The Constitution explicitly defines the 'privileges' of Parliament in the main text
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is the presiding officer of the Parliament as a whole
practiceMCQs.answer: The President is an integral part of Parliament but does not participate in the business of either house
practiceMCQs.explanation: Article 79 clearly lists the President, the Council of States, and the House of the People as the components of Parliament.

practiceMCQs.question: Regarding the Bicameral nature of the Indian Parliament, which statement is incorrect?
options: Rajya Sabha represents the states, promoting federal balance
Lok Sabha represents the people, providing democratic mandate
Both houses have identical powers regarding the passage of Money Bills
The President can dissolve the Lok Sabha but not the Rajya Sabha
practiceMCQs.answer: Both houses have identical powers regarding the passage of Money Bills
practiceMCQs.explanation: Under Article 109, Money Bills can only be introduced in the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha has very limited powers regarding them; it cannot reject or amend them.
